connection: Session 17 left working concrete repositories in Domain and App can construct them directly. This session extracts one honest interface from ClockEntryRepository's existing public methods; it does not pretend that services, policy classes, or multiple implementations already exist.
objectives: Explain an interface as a contract that lists required members without owning the implementation.
Extract IClockEntryRepository from the three public operations ClockEntryRepository already provides.
Make ClockEntryRepository satisfy that contract without changing its behavior.
Use an interface-typed variable and explain what is replaceable now and what is not yet built.

visuals.title: Extract the contract from working behavior
visuals.explanation: IClockEntryRepository repeats the signatures already used to save an entry, query completed entries, and locate an open entry. No speculative service API is invented.

visuals.title: The implementation still does the work
visuals.explanation: The interface contains no List and no method bodies. ClockEntryRepository retains the private collection and implements each operation.

visuals.title: Declared type versus runtime object
visuals.explanation: IClockEntryRepository repository = new ClockEntryRepository(); exposes only the contract while the runtime object remains ClockEntryRepository.

visuals.title: One implementation is enough to learn the boundary
visuals.explanation: There is only one implementation today. The interface creates a substitution seam for later tests or persistence; it does not prove that a second implementation already exists.

preQuiz.prompt: Where should the members of IClockEntryRepository come from?
options: The public repository behavior the application already uses
Every method on every domain class
preQuiz.explanation: Extracting an interface from working behavior keeps the contract small and truthful.

preQuiz.prompt: Does an interface-typed variable construct an interface object?
options: No; it still refers to an object created from a concrete class
Yes; interfaces are constructed with new
preQuiz.explanation: The declared type controls visible capabilities; the concrete object supplies the implementation.

preQuiz.prompt: How many IClockEntryRepository implementations exist at the start of this lab?
preQuiz.explanation: The lesson must describe the learner's real code, not a future architecture.

concept.title: An interface states a contract
paragraphs: An interface says which operations an implementation must provide. It does not store the repository List or explain how those operations work.
Use the exact signatures already present on ClockEntryRepository so the abstraction follows real behavior.

concept.title: The concrete repository implements the contract
paragraphs: Adding : IClockEntryRepository asks the compiler to verify that ClockEntryRepository supplies every required member with a compatible signature.
The methods and private collection do not need to move into the interface.

concept.title: Polymorphism starts with the caller's view
paragraphs: An interface-typed variable can refer to any object that implements the interface. Today it refers to ClockEntryRepository; later a test double or database repository could occupy the same slot.
This session creates the boundary only. Session 20 gives a service a genuine reason to depend on it.

concept.title: Architecture note — contract inside, implementation outside
paragraphs: The course leaves both files in Domain for now so this lesson can focus on interfaces. That is a teaching simplification, not the recommended final production layout.

In a larger solution, IClockEntryRepository stays on the inner side, usually in Domain or Application, while ClockEntryRepository commonly moves to Infrastructure/Repositories. Application and Infrastructure may reference Domain; Domain never references Infrastructure. App is the outer composition root that selects the concrete implementation.
concept.code:
Application  ──▶ Domain
Infrastructure ──▶ Domain
App ──▶ Application + Infrastructure
Domain ──X─▶ Infrastructure

lab.objective: Extract one accurate repository interface from code that already works, then use that contract from App.
lab.startingCondition: Domain contains ClockEntryRepository with SaveClockEntry, GetEmployeeClockEntries, and GetOpenClockEntry. No repository interface or production service exists yet.
lab.keyPointTitle: Do not invent abstractions ahead of behavior
keyPoints: Copy signatures, not method bodies, into the interface.
Keep repository storage private inside ClockEntryRepository.
Use one interface now; services and additional implementations arrive only when a later lesson creates a reason.
steps: Open Repositories/ClockEntryRepository.cs and list its three public methods.
Confirm _clockEntries remains private so the interface does not expose storage.
Create IClockEntryRepository.cs in the Domain project.
Use the same namespace as ClockEntryRepository.
Add the SaveClockEntry signature without copying its body.
Add the GetEmployeeClockEntries signature with its existing parameter and return types.
Add the GetOpenClockEntry signature, including the nullable ClockEntry? return type.
Build to catch any signature or namespace mistakes before changing the class.
Add : IClockEntryRepository to the ClockEntryRepository declaration.
Build again and let the compiler verify all three members.
Open App/Program.cs and preserve every earlier session section.
Append a clearly labeled Session 18 section.
Declare an IClockEntryRepository variable and assign a new ClockEntryRepository to it.
Call one existing repository operation through the interface variable.
Explain in a comment why repository-specific members would not be visible through that variable.

steps.text: Run App, then build and test the solution. Open the solution only after making your own attempt.
steps.code:
dotnet run --project src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App.csproj --configuration Release
dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release && dotnet test PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release --no-build

reveals.title: Solution
reveals.text: Compare the contract and implementation declaration with your work. Keep your existing repository method bodies and earlier Program.cs sections.

lab.expectedBehavior: The repository still behaves exactly as before, the compiler confirms it satisfies IClockEntryRepository, and App calls it through the interface contract.
lab.validation: dotnet run --project src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App.csproj --configuration Release && dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release && dotnet test PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release --no-build

expectedFiles.why: Declare the existing repository operations as one contract.
Declare that the concrete repository implements the contract.
Exercise the repository through an interface-typed variable.
Keep the lesson synchronized with the real cumulative build.

review: The interface matches the three existing repository signatures.
No service, employee interface, policy hierarchy, or second implementation is claimed to exist.
Earlier production code and ScratchPad experiments remain intact.

postQuiz.prompt: What does : IClockEntryRepository add to ClockEntryRepository?
options: A compiler-checked promise that the class supplies the contract
postQuiz.explanation: The class still owns the implementation; the compiler checks the promised members.

postQuiz.prompt: Why not create four interfaces in this session?
options: Only the clock-entry repository has been selected as a real boundary needed by the next session
postQuiz.explanation: A small honest abstraction is easier to understand than speculative architecture.

postQuiz.prompt: What can later replace ClockEntryRepository without changing an interface-based consumer?
postQuiz.explanation: Interface polymorphism depends on satisfying the contract, not inheriting the implementation.

reflections: Which repository details remain deliberately hidden from IClockEntryRepository?
Why is having only one implementation today not proof that the interface is fake?
What evidence would justify extracting another interface later?
whatBreaks: If a signature in IClockEntryRepository differs from the existing method, ClockEntryRepository cannot satisfy the contract. If App declares the variable as ClockEntryRepository instead, behavior still works but the caller is coupled to that concrete implementation.
summary: Session 18 extracts one truthful IClockEntryRepository contract from the three operations already implemented by ClockEntryRepository. The concrete repository keeps its private storage and behavior; App merely narrows its view to the interface. Services and alternate implementations are not claimed to exist yet.
